intro: Murs is a hill village in the Vaucluse, on the edge of the Monts de Vaucluse above the Luberon valley, among fields, cherry orchards and stone farmhouses. Just outside it, on the verge of a narrow lane, stands a downy oak with a squat grey trunk and a crown far wider than it is tall. A reader sent us its photographs and puts it at 600 to 1,000 years old.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this downy oak from the countryside just outside Murs, a hill village on the edge of the Monts de Vaucluse, and put it at 600 to 1,000 years old with a trunk about six metres round.

Those figures are theirs, not a measurement or a register we have seen, but the photographs explain why they think so. The trunk is a great grey column of cracked, scaly bark, flaring at the foot into knuckled roots that grip the bank like toes. At about head height it splits into three huge limbs, one of them reaching far out sideways over the verge, and above them the crown spreads into a broad dome much wider than it is tall, copper and gold in the November light.

Downy oak, Quercus pubescens, is the oak of Provence's dry hills and truffle grounds. It keeps its dead leaves into winter, which is why the reader's tree is still clothed when the cherries and walnuts around it are bare. Old ones are often left standing alone at field edges, as this one is, beside a narrow lane with stone farmhouses on the slope behind.

If you know this tree's name or its story in the village, tell us here and we will add it. Walk under the outstretched limb to stand beside the trunk.

question_meta: A huge downy oak beside a lane outside Murs in the Vaucluse, sent by a reader who puts it at 600 to 1,000 years: where it stands.
question_answer: The Great Downy Oak of Murs stands on the verge of a narrow lane in the fields just outside Murs, in the Vaucluse. It can be seen from the lane at any time.
question_context: A reader who sent us this tree from the fields just outside Murs, a hill village on the edge of the Monts de Vaucluse, puts it at 600 to 1,000 years old and its trunk at about six metres round. Neither figure comes from a register or a measurement we have seen, so they are the reader's own. Their photographs show a downy oak, Quercus pubescens, the oak of Provence's dry hills, standing alone on the verge of a narrow paved lane. The trunk is a squat grey column of cracked bark on knuckled roots, and at about head height it splits into three huge limbs, one of them reaching far out sideways over the verge. Above them the crown makes a dome much wider than it is tall, and because downy oaks keep their dead leaves into winter it was still copper and gold in late November, when the cherry trees around it were bare. Stone farmhouses stand on the slope behind. It stands beside a public lane, so it can be seen from the road at any time; we have not confirmed who owns the field.

faq.q: Can I visit The Great Downy Oak of Murs?
faq.a: Yes, from the lane. It stands on the verge of a narrow public lane outside the village; we have not confirmed who owns the field behind it.

faq.q: How old is the downy oak at Murs?
faq.a: The reader who sent it puts it at 600 to 1,000 years. We have no register or measured figure for it yet.

faq.q: When is the oak at Murs at its best?
faq.a: In late autumn its crown turns copper and gold, and a downy oak keeps those leaves well into winter.
